title: How to Plan a Retirement Budget That Actually Works
description: Using the 'Smile' spending curve to forecast expenses.
content:
The most common retirement budgeting mistake is assuming your spending will be flat, adjusted for inflation, every year until you die. Real life doesn't work that way. Retirement spending typically follows a 'Smile' or 'U-Curve'. Spending is high in the early years (travel/fun), drops in the middle years (slowing down), and spikes in the final years (healthcare/long-term care). Building a budget that matches this reality prevents you from over-saving for a middle age you won't enjoy or under-saving for a late age you need to fund.

Key Takeaways

  • The 'Go-Go' Years (65-75): You have health and time. Spending often equals or exceeds pre-retirement levels due to travel and hobbies. Budget 100-110% of current spend.
  • The 'Slow-Go' Years (75-85): Activity slows. One car is sold. Travel becomes local. Spending drops to ~70-80% of baseline (inflation adjusted).
  • The 'No-Go' Years (85+): Health declines. Spending spikes due to medical needs, assisted living, or home care. This is the expensive end of the smile.
  • Inflation Nuance: Seniors face different inflation. Electronics get cheaper, but healthcare gets expensive. Your personal inflation rate might be higher than CPI.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Medicare does not cover 'Custodial Care' (nursing homes). This is the biggest shock in the 'No-Go' years. A semi-private room averages $100,000/year. Your budget must have a 'Long-Term Care' sinking fund or insurance policy.

Building the Line Items

Forget your current budget. Build a new one from zero.

1. Subtract Work Costs

  • Commuting (Gas/Train).
  • Professional Wardrobe.
  • Retirement Contributions (You stop saving).
  • FICA Taxes (7.65% raise immediately).

2. Add Retirement Costs

  • Health Insurance: $300-$500/mo for Medicare B+D+Medigap per person.
  • Travel/Leisure: $5,000 - $10,000/year.
  • Home Services: You might hire a lawn service or cleaner as you age.

3. The Tax Estimate

Withdrawals from Traditional 401(k)s are taxable. If you need $6,000/mo to live, you might need to withdraw $7,500/mo to cover federal/state taxes. Don't forget the IRS.

Testing the Budget

  1. The 'Practice Year': One year before retiring, live strictly on your projected retirement budget. Can you do it? If it feels tight, work another year to build a bigger cushion.
  2. The 'One-Time' Bucket: Separate recurring expenses (Utilities) from one-time expenses (New Roof/New Car). Keep a separate cash fund for the lumpy items so they don't break your monthly flow.
  3. Review Annually: Inflation is not uniform. If your property taxes jump 10%, you need to cut from the Travel budget. Be dynamic.
  4. The 'Fun' Floor: Budget for fun. If you don't allocate money for joy, you will hoard cash and die the richest person in the graveyard. Spend your dividends.

Frequently Asked Questions

What if I spend too much early on?

That's okay, as long as it's planned. Spending 5% of your portfolio at age 65 to travel is fine if you plan to drop to 3% at age 75. Just don't spend 5% forever.

How do I budget for nursing homes?

This is a catastrophic risk. Either buy LTC insurance, or plan to sell your home to fund it. Do not try to fund a $100k/year liability from monthly cash flow.

Does downsizing save money?

Sometimes. Moving to a condo lowers maintenance but raises HOA fees. Run the numbers. The savings is usually in releasing home equity, not monthly cash flow.
